The Nineteenth Amendment. In 1920, the United States Constitution was amended to grant women the right to vote nationwide. This wasn't a sudden decision—it came after decades of suffrage activism led by figures like Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton. The amendment marked a watershed moment in American democracy and women's rights, instantly expanding the electorate by roughly twenty million women.

The story of how it happened is worth knowing. The amendment was ratified on August eighteenth, nineteen twenty, after the Tennessee legislature cast the deciding vote. But the real pressure had come years earlier. In eighteen seventy-two, Susan B. Anthony was arrested for voting illegally, and that arrest energized the movement and kept Congress under pressure. By the time the amendment passed, some states had already granted women's suffrage on their own, but the amendment ended the patchwork of state-by-state systems. Wyoming had been the first territory to do so, all the way back in eighteen sixty-nine.

The amendment's language was simple. "The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied on account of sex." But those words belied decades of struggle. Opponents had warned of chaos and the collapse of traditional gender roles, yet somehow political stability endured. The amendment was connected to the broader women suffrage movement and the progressive era that made its passage possible.
